claims.text: The studied material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy in nanoscale thin-film or patterned-nanoribbon form.
The as-deposited material has a fine-grained, defect-rich microstructure.
Interface-induced domain-wall pinning primarily controls the low-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis.
A high density of grain boundaries and deposition-induced defects creates local magnetic anisotropies.
These local anisotropies and pinning sites slow reversible magnetic transitions.
The grain boundaries and deposition-induced defects impede efficient heat transfer during cycling.
Rapid thermal annealing can promote controlled grain growth and reduce grain-boundary and defect density.
Grain size and boundary density mediate domain-wall pinning and local magnetic anisotropy.
Reducing interfaces and defect pinning centers facilitates more uniform and reversible magnetic transitions.
Improved inter-grain magnetic coupling after annealing aids heat transfer and partially mitigates cycle-frequency limits.
Annealed films or nanoribbons will exhibit lower hysteresis than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed films or nanoribbons will exhibit lower coercivity than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will produce a more pronounced and sharper magnetocaloric peak.
Reduced pinning will allow magnetic domains to reverse more readily under applied fields below 0.1 T.
The as-deposited baseline has substantial domain-wall pinning and sluggish thermal response.
The proposed mechanism applies to geometries with nanoscale features below 100 nm and applied fields below 0.1 T.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to thicker films or bulk materials, where other microstructural or heat-transfer mechanisms may prevail.
